content.title: About
content.content: Saccharin is an artificial sweetener about 300–400 times sweeter than sugar but contains no calories. The liquid form is convenient for adding to drinks, sauces, baked goods and confectionery. It is heat‑stable and has a long shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Saccharin was discovered in 1879 by German chemist Constantin F. Fahlberg.
Originally it was used medically as a cough suppressant and for diabetes treatment.
In the 1970s the United States imposed a temporary ban on saccharin over cancer concerns, but later studies lifted the restriction.
Liquid saccharin is widely used in soft drinks and energy beverages.
Saccharin does not affect blood glucose levels, making it suitable for diabetic products.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Saccharin provides sweetness without adding calories, helping with weight‑management diets.

items.title: Does not raise blood sugar
items.content: The sweetener has a zero glycemic index, making it safe for people with diabetes.

items.title: Heat stability
items.content: Saccharin retains its sweetness during cooking and baking, useful for a wide range of recipes.

items.title: Bitter aftertaste
items.content: At high concentrations saccharin can leave a characteristic bitter aftertaste.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergy symptoms such as itching, rash or swelling.

items.title: Children’s intake
items.content: Because it may influence taste preferences, saccharin consumption should be limited for young children.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 1–2 drops of liquid saccharin per 100 ml of beverage, sauce, marinade or batter. In baking it replaces sugar at a ratio of about 1 : 300–400 (by sweetness).

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For long‑term storage check for sediment or off‑odors before use.
